I'm Jackson Hurley, and my submission is <https://episteme.wiki|episteme.wiki>. It's a live, hosted implementation of the core of the epistemic stack, including ingestion and canonicalization of claims, assessment, structuring into arguments and subclaims, through to serving the claim graph via website, browser extension, and API/MCP.

- From: VJ <vaibhavjain137@gmail.com> (ID: U0BBUEEL19T) 
  Message_ts: 1784521764.710109
  Sharing my submission: *Calibration as Linkage Integrity*

The core claim is that a knowledge base's rigor is not a property of the base, it is a property of what the base does to a reasoner leaning on it. A base can be well-structured and well-sourced and still make a competent reader double-count correlated evidence or lean on a withdrawn claim. You cannot see that by inspecting the base and will only show up in the reader.

So I built an instrument that measures it. `epistack_eval.py` runs in one command, sends real reasoners through a base under a knowledge mask and reports whether they double-count, miss the crux, or lean on retracted evidence. The base is an input, so it points at any base, including anyone else's here.

I built a real 26-claim COVID-origins base by deep research on two models, reconciled it, stripped out the correlation flags and hid them as an answer key, then ran the instrument on the flat version. It independently re-derived the five-claim Wuhan cluster and showed a reasoner double-counting it, in every one of fourteen runs.

It also has a repair loop that collapses the cluster and re-measures to confirm the fix, and the check caught its own first repair overshooting before a weight-preserving one landed.

Early feedback steer, to push past the argument and actually operationalise "calibration per reader effort" into something like an Epistack Eval, is what helped me shape this.

That is exactly the direction I took it, and where I want to keep building.

Repo and one-command demo in the full submission here <https://github.com/vaibhav-labs/Epistack_Eval|github.com/vaibhav-labs/Epistack_Eval> . Happy to point it at your base if it is useful.

Absolutely loved working on it !

  Dear all,

I wish you all good luck with your submissions!
I represent a different discipline to data science and software engineering here – my expertise lies in HCI (Human Computer Interaction).

I submitted a contribution under the "Other" category, which I am sharing as <https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ssedHn5jFqacV1hwZEy6KNFa3FxsrZFY/view?usp=sharing|Interactive visualization tool for knowledge  mapping & creation with AI (PDF)>. There was no email confirmation/copy of the submission – so I hope it went through!

This is a high level design concept, a vision for *interactive visualisation tools* that enable users to explore claims with *large amounts of data* and better *understand the evolution of discourse over time*. It proposes an alternative to network/ spider diagrams through a *clustering mechanism*. Sources/ evidence for the same or similar claim are clustered in one "claim plane" and the user can zoom in/out between "everything" and specific claims. The objectives are to reduce cognitive load and to enable *human-AI knowledge creation through dynamic pathways*, where the 'human' can initiate a path as a new branch at various levels (topic/ subtopic/ claim description).
I have been exploring two different approaches:
1. *"Chrono"*: a scalable tool for controversial (i.e. Covid origins) and *complex* (i.e. black holes) topics that *evolve over time*
2. *"Diverse"*: when the topic is *very broad* and it first requires mapping (i.e. eggs & human health). This idea builds up on what current LLMs can do today.

As I was drawing this, it reminded me of my summer PhD internship at MIT's Media Lab in 2005, with the Sociable Media Group (Dr Judith Donath) at the time – which later became The Social Computing Group. About 20 years ago, we were designing experimental interactive visualisations that helped users feel connectedness, identify relationships and make sense of large amounts of social media data.

What I shared here are early stage design ideas, sketches, which could evolve into working prototypes, if a team is interested in exploring this further. I would be interested to hear thoughts of this attempt – beyond the scope of the contest. And if there is something here that also has some merit for your work – I would love to know!

Thank you all and good luck!
Yanna

Hi everyone, I was looking into making the competition's three-layer framework (ingestion, structure, assessment) something that can be seen and walked through, so I made a map in IcePanel.

It's meant to be an ideal-type schematic based on the contest materials alone. Since we have all been building to a common specification, perhaps it will provide a helpful way to think about Epistack projects.

The top level of the schematic shows how evidence, people, and AI interact with the stack from the outside, and you can zoom into boxes to get down to individual components. Sharing it here in case it's useful to anyone thinking through system architecture. I'd genuinely welcome corrections where something seems mapped wrong.

<https://s.icepanel.io/ltO4ZvaTDdblNc/TNZ7|s.icepanel.io/ltO4ZvaTDdblNc/TNZ7>

• Where to start: click the magnifying-glass icon on any box to drill down. The three layers each open into their components (claim extraction, inference resolution, crux identification, etc.). There's also a tag overlay for seven contest criteria, so you can highlight which parts of the system speak to, say, adversarial robustness or compounding.

• There's a flow called "A claim's journey" that traces a single real claim (a furin cleavage site argument) through the whole stack, from ingestion to crux surfacing. Use the Next button or arrow keys to move through the steps.

The live copy can be extended. If you'd like edit access, please DM me your email and I'll add you. It's still an early draft and rough in places. Hope it's a helpful starting point for others too.

Hello everyone,

Now that the contest is ended, I know we are all thinking about next steps. For me, it's been about general approaches to improving knowledge graphs, making investigations understandable at a glance, and also the continuing challenge of how to improve upon off-the-shelf Claude Code.

1. There are neurosymbolic approaches to knowledge graphs with impressive potential that might be worth working on. They use techniques from formal logic. My searching indicates that while implemented into ontologies like Amazon's product labels and descriptions, they have yet to break through to the consumer side to drive better conclusions, despite logic formally governing valid arguments. The most prominent library I could find relating to this seems to be IBM's Logical Neural Networks and I thought I would share their repo here: <https://github.com/IBM/LNN|github.com/IBM/LNN>
2. Visuals representing knowledge graphs that use boxes of text and connections can and should be made to be user-friendly and understandable by design. How far can the envelope be pushed towards an interface so natural as to approach the ambitions, for instance, of some of our finest filmmakers and game makers? :sweat_smile:
3. It seems to me that off-the-shelf Claude Code will largely be a function of prompt and context. By function, I imagine something similar to a mathematical function that takes a set of definite inputs (which can be large and varied) and yields an output (often sprawling and hard to digest). There might be an illuminating analogy to be drawn here. Goedel's Incompleteness Theorems show that a static set of axioms can never produce all the truths of mathematics: there will always be extra-system propositions not provable from within the system, with new axioms needing to be brought in to prove concrete system-unprovable claims, resetting the cycle. If the analogy holds, further work on the Epistack might wish to attend to the "unheard voices" and perspectives not derivable from initial prompts themselves. I noticed at least one project - Epistemic Evidence Review - that does this quite well. Improvements that accommodate claim-level human feedback (I made a try at this) might yield the kind of search steering needed to span the gap. May the eventual stack fully fill it.

Best wishes everyone! I know I'd love discussing the Meta-Epistack.

  Hi all!
We think that we might have exposed a serious flaw in LLM-enhanced argument mining pipelines. For our entry we've conducted some preliminary experiments to verify that and got positive results. But the scale of the experiments is pretty meager and we're still not sure whether the results apply to real production pipelines. Anyone ready to run a simple experiment on their own pipeline?

Just run your pipeline on the same text with the same settings 30 times and check whether the results have diverging epistemic consequences: say, jointly they allow to draw inconsistent conclusions, or they picture the sides of the debate differently each time. If so, that would mean an epistemically important instability.

Here is the setup in which we show that such situations are possible. LLM extracts arguments and relations of two kinds (attack/support) from a text. Those constitute a graph. After that a Bipolar semantic is used to compute labels for each argument (accepted/rejected). We do that 30 times with Sonnet 5 on the first section of Scott Alexander's write-up on COVID. After that we use MiniLM embeddings to cluster 'the same' arguments from different runs into families to make different graphs comparable. Then we check how many of the arguments in a family have the same labels across runs. If they all have the same, the family is stable. Otherwise it's unstable. In this experiment 33 out of 79 families were unstable. We've used PageRank to determine families that are 'important' for the debate structure. 6 of the 33 unstable families had PageRang in the top 25%. Among those, for example, this argument: 'COVID started spreading quietly weeks to months before the first market-related case was detected.' In most runs this argument is rejected, but in some - accepted, so the pipeline produces unstable results.

We really want to further this line of research for two reasons:
1. If such a problem exists, it poses serious concerns for the validity of results of such pipelines;
2. Any experimental results at this point will be both philosophically and practically interesting. We'd love to be proved wrong.

Detailed methodology and supporting experiments can be found in our project folder.
<https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/10X2H7CLyAlOYHfYdeBQpeaSQ8HxHFqb0?usp=sharing|drive.google.com/drive/folders/…?usp=sharing>

I think we discussed about this in another thread with other members of the community, glat to see your results <@U0BEDN2DPPG|Andrey Zdanevich>.

1. I do think there is value on testing inter-run stability, and I think this path is a nice step forward! I still think that the problem is much bigger than it looks. Ideally we would want to know which model, under which prompt, works best for which kind of subject matter, and that likely varies across disciplines and across tasks (a model may be stronger at, say, methodology extraction than relation labelling).
The point is also that as an outside of domain reader, one cannot fairly evaluate where the model is being too generic or plainly wrong.  One needs a domain expert to tell you where the non-deterministic behaviour breaks something and where it does not matter.
In our own annotation work this showed up: on 178 question pairs from a male-fertility corpus, two PhD-level annotators reached only 0.747 observed agreement (Cohen's κ 0.506, Gwet's AC1 0.710) and the disagreement was not about direction, but about whether two questions were the same question at all. We also saw that out-of-domain annotators marked as correct what in-domain ones flagged as real errors, including polarity inversions (the model reporting the opposite direction of the stated effect), so apparent model accuracy went up simply because the annotator could not see the mistakes.

Without expert judges I think it is hard to know the limits of what one is measuring. What i mean is that relevancy and stability in LLMs are two different tasks, and I believe one may confound the other. That is, a run can be highly stable and still be systematically wrong, in which case stability ends up measuring consistency in error rather than quality of content extraction.
This is not an easy problem to isolate and empirically study, and  I believe experiments in both directions are relevant, for sure.

2. On whether the structure should rest on labels like contradicts or entails, I am unsure, as I tried different labels and experiments in this line:
• Option 1: entailment, contradiciton, neutral (the classical NLI framing)
• Option 2: same, compatible, contradicts, quantitative divergence, distinct
I only had one dataste, and  the richer schema did not clearly help. Option 1 did better on some cases and option 2 on others.
But the more interesting finding was where both break. We benchmarked relation classification on SciFact (evidence-claim) and on the ManCon corpus (claim-claim contradictions in cardiovascular abstracts). With a pre-registered bar of accuracy >= 0.70, several models clear it on evidence-claim pairs, but on ManCon's claim-claim pairs none of them do. Models default to _neutral_ almost everywhere, and larger reasoning models don't repair it at acceptable cost. Reframing the prompt toward agreement raised entailment recall on SciFact but didn't close the claim-claim gap.
That may matter for your setup: claim–claim relation labelling is where classifiers are weakest, and it's exactly the layer your results identify as the least stable. So part of what you're measuring as instability may be the classifier having no confident answer to give, rather than the model changing its mind between runs. Distinguishing 'unstable because the task is hard' from 'unstable because the model is noisy' seems like a valuable next step.
Also, I would say that the label ontology itself is still an open question, and further work must be done in this direction (that is, optimizing relevant information extraction with LLMs).

The two things that helped us most were: a) picking an existing dataset whose task is genuinely the same as yours rather than approximately similar. To know whether a model has systematic tendencies rather than random noise, you would want repeated runs on the same input (pass@k style), as <@U0BEDN2DPPG|Andrey Zdanevich> mentioned. On top of that you need qualitative error analysis by domain experts, because an out-of-domain reader cannot tell where the classification is subtly off. This is difficult to put together in terms of resources.

For the particular task of quality of knowledge extraction, I would start small with experts, like using LLMs to extract knowledge form N papers and then sit with experts to analyse exactly where the errors are, and whether it is a prompt issue that few-shot examples fix, or something deeper (that is why I mentioned interpretabilty on AI reasoning before).
All this in parallel trying to improve reasoning in LLMs, as that may partly fix the problem.
I also sometimes wonder whether we are asking too much of current LLM capabilities, and whether the next generation of architectures (beyond transformers) might close some of this gap. Or maybe chain-of-thought will prove more powerful than we expect, who knows!

  <@U0BCBF6P24D|z3os> There are two very fine points you've made at the start of the discussion which have to be approached with appropriate subtlety.

Our work is focused on exploring just one feature of the LLM-enhanced argument mining pipeline: variability. The whole post-LLM pipeline is really just a measuring instrument for epistemic impact. Your next point perfectly illustrates how task description should be considered when we talk about validity. My point is that the impact of variability on the pipeline output should be accounted for _in the context of your pipeline's task_.

Epistemic instability caused by variability is an indicator of low quality of the produced graphs (relative to the task), because it means that some of them are more wrong than others, and you don't know which ones. But simply reducing it does not guarantee better graphs. Specifically (it has been already pointed out by <@U0BBST7TYUV|Lidia Salas Espejo>) the intermodel consensus might settle around systemic errors. That is why battling variability is not a trivial task. We are incredibly interested in new ideas on that problem: if you decide to reduce the variability instead of exploiting it, how to do it in such a way that improves the output quality of the pipeline?

Our idea is to draw upon the symbolic roots of argument mining and reduce variability by imposing strict verification processes the graphs have to pass. This would simultaneously reduce the number of epistemically divergent graphs, measurably improve the pipeline output quality and make the pipeline more explainable.
